name: Mazda 717C
hook: Mazda's first real Le Mans prototype started 44th, finished 12th, and won its class on the class's very first outing.
story: June 1983. Le Mans has a brand-new class for small prototypes, called Group C Junior. Mazda turns up with its first proper sports prototype, the 717C. It is a little thing. Behind the driver hums a twin-rotor engine of just 1.3 litres. The chassis and body come from Mooncraft, a small Japanese shop, working with Mazda. Car 60 qualifies 44th. Nobody is watching it. Its crew are Yoshimi Katayama, Yojiro Terada and Takashi Yorino. The race grinds on through the night. Engines let go. Cars limp into the pits and stay there. The little Mazda just keeps spinning, lap after lap. When the flag falls, car 60 is twelfth overall and first in its class. Its sister car, with Steve Soper, James Weaver and Jeff Allam, comes home eighteenth. They are the only two cars in the class to finish. Twelfth was the best result yet for a Japanese entry at Le Mans. Eight years later, a rotary Mazda would win the whole race.
description: The 717C was Mazda's first purpose-built sports prototype, made for the new Group C Junior class of 1983. Mooncraft built the chassis and bodywork with Mazda's help. Power came from a 13B two-rotor rotary engine of 1,308 cc. Mazdaspeed entered two cars at the 1983 Le Mans 24 Hours, and they finished 12th and 18th overall, first and second in class, the only class finishers. The 727C replaced it in 1984.
